29:1.text: Therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvellous work among this people, even a marvellous work and a wonder: for the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hid.

provenance.route: Isaiah 29:14 → KJV → Book of Mormon (transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 27:26)
provenance.other: “proceed to do a marvellous work” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:14. 'Marvellous work' alone occurs in five, four of them Chronicles and Psalms in the plural 'marvellous works'; only Isaiah 29:14 has the singular with 'proceed to do'. The Book of Mormon's own transcription at 2 Nephi 27:26 keeps the KJV's 'among this people'; 29:1 changes it to 'among them'.
provenance.significance: Chapter 29 is spoken in the Lord's voice and opens by quoting the verse that has been its warrant since chapter 27: the marvellous work of Isaiah 29:14 is, in this book's reading, the coming forth of the record. What the source supplies and the quotation withholds is the rest of the sentence — 'the wisdom of their wise men shall perish' — which 2 Nephi 27:26 does give in full, and which is the judgment 29:3's Gentiles are about to earn by saying there cannot be any more Bible. The oracle they are standing under is the one about wisdom perishing.

29:1.note: The opening clause reproduces a KJV singleton exactly except for its object, and the object is the change worth noting: Isaiah's work is done 'among this people' — Jerusalem — while 29:1's is done 'among them', the many at that day, which the rest of the verse identifies as the house of Israel scattered. This is the Lord resuming, in his own voice, the text his prophet has just transcribed. The pairing with Isaiah 11:11 in the same sentence is treated as a separate link.

29:1.text: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.

provenance.route: Isaiah 11:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon (transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 21:11)
provenance.other: “set his hand again the second time” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:11, and “recover the remnant” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. 2 Nephi 21:11's transcription is verbally identical to the KJV at both points, so nothing here distinguishes the biblical route from the internal one.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 11:11 is the verse this whole chapter is an argument about. Its second recovery gathers the remnant from eight named places ending 'from the islands of the sea', and 29:7 and 29:11 will both press that ending: if the Lord recovers people from the islands of the sea, he has people there, and if he has people there he has spoken to them. The Gentile objection at 29:3 is answered out of the geography of a verse the book has already transcribed. Recover Isaiah 11 and one sees why the chapter cites it twice and closes on Abraham's seed: 11:12's ensign gathers 'the outcasts of Israel' and 'the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth', which is 29:11-14's east, west, north, south and gathering home.

29:1.note: Two KJV singletons in one clause. The Book of Mormon's change is 'my people, which are of the House of Israel' for Isaiah's 'the remnant of his people, which shall be left' — first person for third, since the Lord is speaking, and the standing Book of Mormon formula for the house of Israel in place of Isaiah's remnant. Isaiah 11 stands transcribed in this book eight chapters earlier at 2 Nephi 21, and that transcription reads exactly as the KJV here, so the mediation cannot be decided from the wording and is recorded as direct-OT rather than guessed at OT-via-earlier-BoM. Compare 29:14 at 28:14, where the same test did yield an answer.

29:2.text: And he will lift up an ensign to the nations from far, and will hiss unto them from the end of the earth: and, behold, they shall come with speed swiftly:

provenance.route: Isaiah 5:26 + Isaiah 49:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon; both verses stand transcribed or quoted earlier in this book, at 2 Nephi 15:26 and 2 Nephi 6:6
provenance.other: The KJV hisses in exactly two verses, Isaiah 5:26 and Zechariah 10:8, and only Isaiah 5:26 hisses toward the end of the earth. “set up my standard” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 49:22; 'standard' as a signal raised for a people occurs otherwise only at Isaiah 59:19 and 62:10.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis reverses the direction of the summons. In Isaiah 5:26 the hissing calls a distant army down on Judah — it is the last verse before the invaders arrive with speed swiftly — and in 29:2 it is the Lord's words that hiss forth to the ends of the earth, so that the sound which summoned destroyers now summons readers. Isaiah 49:22's standard is set up to gather the exiles' sons and daughters, and Jacob has already quoted that verse in this book at 2 Nephi 6:6 for exactly that purpose. 29:2 fuses the two signals: the hiss from Isaiah 5 and the standard from Isaiah 49, both aimed at the same house of Israel.

29:2.note: Two Isaiah signals joined in a sentence about a book. 'Hiss' is the rarer and the odder — a modern reader hears derision where the KJV means a whistle for attention — and its appearance here, with 'unto the ends of the earth', places Isaiah 5:26 rather than Zechariah 10:8. What makes the row more than a phrase-match is that both source verses are already inside this book: Isaiah 5:26 transcribed at 2 Nephi 15:26 with the same wording, and Isaiah 49:22 quoted by Jacob at 2 Nephi 6:6. The mediation is left direct-OT because neither internal text differs from the KJV at the words 29:2 uses.

29:4.text: Then he said unto them, O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken:

provenance.other: “O fools, and slow of heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:25, and the bare vocative 'O fools' is that verse's alone as well (Proverbs 13:19's 'abomination to fools' is not a vocative and is addressed to no one). The singular 'Thou fool' at 29:6 occurs in four KJV verses, of which Luke 12:20's is the rich fool this book has already drawn on at 2 Nephi 28:7.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's sharpest recovered context. Luke 24:25 is the risen Christ on the road to Emmaus rebuking two disciples who have the scriptures and cannot read them — 'slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken' — and the rebuke is followed immediately by his expounding 'in all the scriptures the things concerning himself'. 2 Nephi 29:4 addresses the identical fault: Gentiles who possess the Bible and conclude from possessing it that there cannot be any more. Luke's fools are told they have not read what they hold; Nephi's are told they have not asked where they got it. The insult is the same insult, and it comes with the same remedy attached.

29:4.note: Two words, and a rare vocative, doing more work than their length. The case rests on the situation matching as exactly as the wording: in the KJV only Luke 24:25 says 'O fools', and only Luke 24:25 says it to people whose fault is what they do with scripture. Confidence is held at moderate because the vocative is a natural thing for a rebuke to reach for, and because the second half of Luke's sentence is not quoted. The verse's other pressure — 'what thank they the Jews' — is registered separately as a Lucan echo at Luke 6:32.

29:4.text: For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them.

provenance.other: “what thank have ye” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Luke 6:32, 6:33 and 6:34, all in one paragraph of the Sermon on the Plain, and nowhere else in the KJV is 'thank' used as a bare noun in a rhetorical question.
provenance.significance: Luke's triple question asks what credit there is in returning good for good; 29:4 asks the inverse — what thanks the Gentiles have given the Jews for a benefit they never returned. Read against Luke 6, the Gentiles fail a test easier than the one Christ sets: they have not even loved those that loved them.

29:4.note: 'What thank they the Jews for the Bible which they receive from them?' turns the KJV's one idiom for this question inside out — Luke's speaker asks what thank the doer has earned, Nephi's asks what thank the receiver has paid. The syntax 'what thank' plus a rhetorical frame is confined to three adjacent verses of Luke, which is what makes it worth recording at all.
29:4.whyNot: The construction is inverted and the noun is the only shared content word; 'thank' as a noun was ordinary in 1611 and not confined to Luke in period English, so the KJV's monopoly on the idiom may be an accident of the KJV rather than evidence of borrowing. Filed at low, and the reader who takes 29:4's question as free composition is not obviously wrong.

29:5.text: Behold, I will raise them out of the place whither ye have sold them, and will return your recompence upon your own head:

provenance.other: “upon your own head” (singular “head”) occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Joel 3:4 and 3:7, where the Lord returns the recompence of Tyre and Zidon on their own head for selling the children of Judah. Acts 18:6 is close in idea — Paul shakes his raiment at the synagogue and says 'Your blood be upon your own heads' before turning to the Gentiles — but its noun is plural, a different phrase, not a third instance of this one.
provenance.significance: Joel 3 is the oracle against the nations that trafficked in Judah, and its charge is precisely 29:5's: 'ye have cursed them, and have hated them, and have not sought to recover them.' Joel's Tyre and Zidon sold the children of Judah to the Grecians and are told their recompence returns on their own head; Nephi's Gentiles received the scriptures from the Jews and cursed them for it. The Acts 18:6 half is the same phrase pointed the other way — there the blood is on the Jews' own heads and Paul departs to the Gentiles — so that the KJV's three occurrences of the idiom hold both halves of the quarrel 2 Nephi 29 is adjudicating. Whether the Book of Mormon intends that symmetry cannot be shown; that the symmetry is there is a fact about the three verses.

29:5.note: 'I will return all these things upon your own heads' has Joel's verb, Joel's preposition and Joel's noun, with 'all these things' standing where Joel has 'your recompence' — a generalisation, since the things being returned are the cursing and hating just listed rather than a price. The verse ends 'for I the Lord, hath not forgotten my people', which answers Isaiah 49:14-15's 'the LORD hath forsaken me… yet will I not forget thee' — a passage Jacob quotes in this book at 2 Nephi 7-8's neighbourhood and which is too diffuse here to catalogue. Confidence moderate: the idiom is a standard prophetic recompense-formula and only its exact KJV wording, confined to three verses, argues for Joel specifically.

29:7.text: Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the fires, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea.

provenance.other: “isles of the sea” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Esther 10:1 and Isaiah 24:15; only Isaiah's are a place where the LORD is glorified. “islands of the sea” — a different phrase — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:11. 29:7 has 'the isles of the sea' and 29:11 has 'the islands of the sea', four verses apart.
provenance.significance: The pair is the finding. The KJV distinguishes two phrases that mean the same thing, and 2 Nephi 29 uses each once, each in the setting its own source supplies: at verse 7 the isles are where the Lord remembers people who are already his, which is Isaiah 24:15's islands glorifying his name, and at verse 11 the islands are the last item in a list of directions from which a scattered people is recovered, which is Isaiah 11:11's. Neither verse could be swapped for the other without losing its source. Isaiah 24 is not among the chapters this book transcribes — 2 Nephi 12-24 covers Isaiah 2-14 — so unlike almost every other borrowing in the chapter this one is reached in the Bible directly.

29:7.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 24:15 at this verse, and the discrimination against Isaiah 11:11 is what makes the row worth writing: an author reaching loosely for a formula would not switch spellings between verse 7 and verse 11 in a way that tracks two different KJV verses. Esther 10:1's isles, a tribute-list, are ruled out by sense. The rest of 29:7 — 'I rule in the heavens above, and in the earth beneath' — is treated as a separate link.

29:7.text: Know therefore this day, and consider it in thine heart, that the LORD he is God in heaven above, and upon the earth beneath: there is none else.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 4:39, with Exodus 20:4's preposition → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “in the earth beneath” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Exodus 20:4, Deuteronomy 5:8 and Acts 2:19 — and Deuteronomy 4:39, whose sense 29:7 has, reads 'upon the earth beneath'. The Book of Mormon has Deuteronomy 4:39's claim in the second commandment's preposition, so no single verse accounts for it.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 4:39 is the KJV's flat statement that the LORD's rule has no geographical limit — 'in heaven above, and upon the earth beneath: there is none else' — and that is the premise 29:7 needs. The Gentile position under attack is territorial: one people, one book, one revelation. The answer is the Shema's neighbourhood, and the question that frames it, 'Know ye not that there are more nations than one?', is Deuteronomy's 'Know therefore this day' turned into a rebuke.

29:7.note: The wording is a fusion and is recorded as such: the sense and the sentence-shape are Deuteronomy 4:39's, the preposition is the second commandment's. Confidence is moderate and `kjvSpecific` uncertain, because 'heaven above and earth beneath' is a formula the KJV repeats in several settings (Joshua 2:11, 1 Kings 8:23) and no one of them is decisively in view. What is not in doubt is that 29:7 is arguing from the universality claim these verses make.

29:8.text: It is also written in your law, that the testimony of two men is true.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 19:15 / 17:6 → John 8:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the testimony of two” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:17, and 2 Nephi 29:8 uses the phrase twice — 'the testimony of two nations is a witness unto you' and 'the testimony of the two nations shall run together'. Deuteronomy 19:15 and 17:6, the underlying law, have neither 'testimony' nor 'two' in this construction: the KJV renders them 'at the mouth of two witnesses'. The Book of Mormon has John's noun, not Moses's.
provenance.significance: John 8:17 is Christ invoking the two-witness law in an argument about whether a single testimony can establish anything — the Pharisees have just said 'Thou bearest record of thyself; thy record is not true', and he answers by adding the Father as the second witness. 2 Nephi 29:8 runs that argument about books rather than persons: one record cannot establish the matter, two can, and the second is supplied by the same God who gave the first. Recover John 8 and the parallel is structural, not decorative. The objectors in both scenes hold the law and use their possession of it to rule out further testimony; in both, the answer is that the law they hold requires a second witness they have refused to hear. The Gentiles of 29:3 say 'we have got a Bible, and there cannot be any more Bible'; John's Pharisees say the same thing about a witness.

29:8.note: A KJV singleton, used twice in one verse, and it settles the mediation cleanly. The two-witness rule is Deuteronomy's, but Deuteronomy's KJV wording is 'at the mouth of two witnesses… shall the matter be established' — no 'testimony', no 'the testimony of two'. That phrase exists in exactly one English verse and it is John's, so the Book of Mormon reaches Deuteronomy through the Gospel rather than directly. Note what the substitution costs and gains: John's two witnesses are persons and 29:8's are nations, which is why the verse has to add the guarantee that the Lord 'speaks the same words unto one nation like unto another' — two witnesses only corroborate if their testimony agrees, and nations, unlike the Father and the Son, might not.

29:11.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

provenance.other: “judged out of those things which were written” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:12, and it is the KJV's only judgment conducted out of the contents of books. “judged every man according to their works” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:13, which 2 Nephi 28:23 has already used.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's argument closed with a hard consequence, and Revelation supplies the mechanism. 29:11's claim is that the Lord commands all men in every quarter to write, 'for out of the books which shall be written, I will judge the world' — which is Revelation 20:12's assize with the plurality of books made the point rather than an incidental detail. If the world is judged out of books, then whose books there are is not a matter of preference. The recovered context also explains why the verse ends 'according to that which is written': in Revelation the written record is what the dead are measured by, so a nation whose record was never made or never received would be judged out of somebody else's books.

29:11.note: Two Revelation 20 verses again, ten chapters after 2 Nephi 28:23 used the same pair for the same assize — there for the fate of the damned, here for the standing of the records. The borrowing is unmistakable at 'judged… according to… works' plus 'out of the books which shall be written', and the Book of Mormon's one substantive change is tense: Revelation's books are already written and opened, and 29:11's are still to be written. That change is the whole chapter in miniature.

29:11.text: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.

provenance.route: Isaiah 11:11-12 → KJV → Book of Mormon (transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 21:11-12)
provenance.other: “islands of the sea” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 11:11, and is the last item in its list of places from which the remnant is recovered — which is exactly where 29:11 puts it, after east, west, north and south. 2 Nephi 21:11's transcription reads 'islands of the sea' identically. The four quarters themselves are Psalm 107:3's 'from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the south', one of exactly two KJV verses with that sequence, the other being Luke 13:29.
provenance.significance: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 11:11 here, and the reason is visible once the two phrases in this chapter are set side by side: 29:7's 'isles of the sea' is Isaiah 24:15's and 29:11's 'islands of the sea' is Isaiah 11:11's, and each sits in the argument its own source fits. Here the point is enumerative — the Lord commands men to write in every direction, and the list ends where Isaiah's list of recovery ends. So the geography of the second gathering becomes the geography of the second scripture. The chapter's whole case is that these are the same map.

29:11.note: Three words, a KJV singleton, and placed at the end of a list of quarters exactly as in the source. The row is written separately from the Isaiah 11:11 quotation at 29:1 because it is a different clause of the source verse doing different work: 29:1 takes the second-time recovery, 29:11 takes the islands. Isaiah 11 stands transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 21 with no departure at either point, so the mediation cannot be told from the wording and is not guessed.

29:14.text: And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee.

provenance.other: 'Everlasting covenant' occurs in fifteen KJV verses and 'thy seed after thee' in a dozen more, so no rarity count supports this row; what supports it is that Genesis 17:7 is the only verse where the covenant with Abraham is made perpetual to his seed, which is the exact claim 29:14 closes on.
provenance.significance: The chapter ends where it must. Its argument has been that the Lord speaks to more nations than one; its danger is that this dissolves the covenant into a general benevolence. Genesis 17:7 is the guard: the covenant is with Abraham 'and thy seed after thee', in perpetuity, so a Lord who speaks to all the nations of the earth has still not stopped being the God of one particular family. That is why 'I covenanted with Abraham that I would remember his seed forever' is the last clause of the chapter and not an appendix to it.

29:14.note: Hardy cross-references Genesis 17:7 here and the reference is sound at the level of substance while carrying almost no wording — 'covenanted with Abraham', 'his seed', 'forever' against Genesis's 'establish my covenant… thy seed after thee… everlasting covenant'. It is written as a moderate allusion rather than either inflated to a quotation or discharged as thematic: the covenant formula is genuinely Genesis 17's and is genuinely being invoked, but nothing in the phrasing could distinguish the KJV from another English Bible, which is why `kjvSpecific` is 'no'.

29:14.text: And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.

provenance.other: “gather together in one” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 11:52 and Ephesians 1:10. John's gathers the scattered children of God, Ephesians' gathers all things in Christ; 29:14 gathers a people to their lands and a word into one, which is John's object rather than Paul's.
provenance.significance: The two halves of 29:14 are the two halves of John 11:52. John's sentence is the evangelist's gloss on Caiaphas — that Jesus would die 'not for that nation only, but… gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad' — which is a statement about one nation's scripture becoming more than one nation's, in a verse about a nation and the others beyond it. That is the subject of 2 Nephi 29 entire. And the neighbouring verse of the same oracle, John 11:50, stands behind 1 Nephi 4:13, where Nephi kills Laban with Caiaphas's sentence; the book returns to the same three verses of John at the moment it argues that its own record belongs with the Jews'.

29:14.note: A two-verse KJV phrase, and the object matches John's rather than Ephesians': what is gathered is a scattered people and their word, not all things in Christ. The row is filed as an echo at moderate because 'gathered in one' is only three words and the Book of Mormon uses gathering language constantly without needing a source for it. What lifts it above coincidence is the recurrence: this book has been in John 11 before, at 1 Nephi 4:13, and the Caiaphas oracle is the New Testament's one passage about a nation's benefit extending past that nation — which is the thesis 29:14 is closing.
29:14.whyNot: Three words, and 'gather in one' is a natural English collocation the KJV happens to use twice. The link is a claim about which of two KJV verses is nearer, made where a third possibility — no source at all — is entirely live.
